readerTitle: Your survey says 83% love you. Who didn't answer?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 업체, B2B 기장·회계 사무소) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 설문 결과는 고객 전체가 아니라 응답한 사람들의 목소리다. 먼저 누가 빠졌는지 묻고, 그다음 평균을 쪼개 본다.
misconception: 응답이 수십 개 이상이고 평균 점수가 높으면 고객 전체가 만족한다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: 표본 선택 편향과 평균의 한계에 관한 통계학 표준 개념 (THK-08-04, THK-08-02)

factChecks.note: 응답률: 지난 1년 고객 480명 중 최근 3개월 예약 고객 300명에게 발송, 60명 응답. 60 ÷ 480 = 12.5%(8명 중 1명), 60 ÷ 300 = 20%.
회계 사무소: 고객 40곳 중 30곳 응답(75%), 평균 8.6/10은 설명용 가정 수치. 가장 큰 고객 3곳 미응답이라는 설정.

cards.title: Your survey says 83% love you. Who didn't answer?
body: A home cleaning company emails a short survey. Sixty customers reply. The average score is 4.3 out of 5, and 83% rate it 4 or 5.
The owner is already drafting a flyer: *"83% of our customers are happy."* Before it goes to print, a few questions are worth asking.

image.label: Cleaner's van with a flyer reading 83% happy
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 청소 업체 밴 옆에서 사장이 "83% happy!"라고 적힌 전단지를 들고 있음. 뒤쪽에 문이 닫힌 집들이 흐릿하게 줄지어 있어 '대답하지 않은 사람들'을 암시. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you check before printing the flyer?
body: The company served 480 customers last year. The survey has 60 replies, a 4.3 average and 83% rating it 4 or 5.
What's the first thing you'd check?

options.text: Who got the survey, and who actually answered it
options.feedback: This is **selection bias** at work. If the people who replied differ from those who didn't, no score tells you about the other 420.

options.text: Nothing. Sixty replies is plenty for a small business
options.feedback: You save time, but the number of replies isn't the problem. Sixty answers from the wrong people can mislead as much as six.

options.text: The average score for each type of job
options.feedback: A strong second step, because **averages hide the story**. But first find out who is missing from the data entirely.

cards.title: The survey only reached part of the business.
body: The survey went to 300 customers with a booking in the last three months. Anyone who stopped booking earlier never saw it. Of those 300, 60 replied.
So the 4.3 speaks for 1 in 8 of last year's customers. And it's not a random 1 in 8. People who left quietly are missing. Those who reply tend to feel strongly, either pleased or upset.
That's **selection bias**: the way data is collected decides who gets counted.

image.label: Funnel: 480 customers, 300 surveyed, 60 replied
image.brief: 깔때기 인포그래픽. 위에서부터 "480 customers last year", "300 got the survey", "60 replied". 깔때기 밖으로 빠져나간 사람 아이콘들에 "Stopped booking", "Didn't reply" 라벨. 차분한 색, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: The 4.3 is made of two very different groups.
body: Here are the 60 replies by score. Most are 5s. But there's a cluster of 1s at the bottom that a single average smooths away.
cards.callout: An average of 4.3 can come from everyone feeling fine, or from most people loving you while a few are furious.

cards.title: One average, two businesses.
body: Split by job type, the picture changes. The 50 weekly regulars average **4.8**. The 10 move-out deep-clean customers average **1.6**. Every 1-star reply came from a move-out job.
This is **averages hide the story**. The blended 4.3 describes nobody. The regulars are delighted, and the move-out service has a real problem that the flyer would have papered over.
cards.softwareNote: In-app surveys have the same trap. The pop-up only reaches people still using the product, so users who churned never vote. Split results by plan or signup month before trusting the average.

cards.title: Don't throw the survey away either.
body: A biased survey still tells you something. The 1-star replies point straight at a fixable problem. Treat skewed data as a lead to check, not a verdict.
Small groups need care. Ten move-out replies is thin, so call a few of those customers before redesigning the service.
And check answers against behavior. Rebookings, cancellations and referrals show what people do, including those who never fill in surveys.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: Your firm does monthly books for 40 small companies. Thirty reply to a survey asking how likely they are to recommend you. The average is 8.6 out of 10.
Your three largest clients, the ones that bring in the most fees, didn't reply. What do you do?

options.text: Report the 8.6 to the partners as good news
options.feedback: Quick and pleasant, but **selection bias** means the clients who matter most to revenue aren't in the number at all.

options.text: Call the silent clients, biggest first, and split scores by client size
options.feedback: You find out who's missing (**selection bias**) and stop small clients from masking big ones (**averages hide the story**). It costs a few calls.

options.text: Resend the survey with a reminder to raise the response rate
options.feedback: More replies help, but reminders often reach the same willing people. Busy large clients usually need a personal call, not another email.

cards.title: A survey speaks only for the people who answered it.
body: You used two ideas: **selection bias** (ask who never got counted) and **averages hide the story** (split the score before you believe it).
**Try it today:** take your latest feedback or reviews. Write down who could have answered, who did, and one way to split the results.
